After death threats were issued against his friend [Salman Rushdie](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Salman-Rushdie) in 1989—following allegations about the sacrilegious nature of Rushdie’s novel _The Satanic Verses_ (1988)—Hitchens publicly defended him, citing his right to freedom of expression and [excoriating](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/excoriating) fellow leftists for failing to do the same. A year later Hitchens released _The Monarchy: A Critique of Britain’s Favorite Fetish_ and _Blood, Class, and Nostalgia: Anglo-American Ironies_ , a discussion of the uneven cultural exchange between the [United States](https://www.britannica.com/place/United-States) and [England](https://www.britannica.com/place/England) . In 1992 he began writing a column for [_Vanity Fair_](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Vanity-Fair-American-magazine) magazine.
